title: Booting macOS on Snapdragon X2 with an EL2 hypervisor
excerpt: Snapintosh runs Apple’s stock kernel on an ASUS Zenbook A16 by emulating Apple silicon contracts at EL2.
body:
A Snapdragon X2-Elite laptop can now run Apple’s macOS 27 (build 26A428), but only because a custom EL2 monitor supplies the exact contracts the kernel expects from Apple silicon. The project, Snapintosh, boots the stock J700/T8140 kernel unmodified and then hands off control to the usual macOS userspace. The result is a full macOS experience on an ASUS Zenbook A16, with the laptop’s native Adreno X2-90 GPU driving the display through a Metal plug-in. The monitor sits between the UEFI firmware and the kernel, translating Apple’s 16 KiB page tables to the hardware’s 4 KiB format and emulating the SPTM and TXM monitor calls the kernel uses for memory management. It also presents the Apple device models the kernel looks for, NVMe, DART, and the GPU ring, so the kernel never knows it is running on a non-Apple platform. The rest of the system, from the USB-C network link that carries boot data to the Adreno driver stack, is built around this contract layer. The following sections break down how the EL2 monitor, the GPU stack, and the USB-C NCM link work together, then finish with a single actionable takeaway. ## EL2 monitor supplies Apple silicon contracts The EL2 monitor is the heart of Snapintosh. Running in the hypervisor layer (EL2), it presents the same set of platform contracts that Apple’s Secure Partition Manager (SPTM) and Trusted Execution Monitor (TXM) provide on A-series chips. Those contracts include: - SPTM/TXM call emulation, allowing the kernel to request services such as secure boot or power management. - Translation of the kernel’s 16 KiB page tables into 4 KiB shadow tables that the Snapdragon hardware can use. - Device tables that describe Apple-specific peripherals like the AIC storage controller, the ANS2 NVMe controller, and the DART IOMMU. - Mediation of the GPU ring and the System Memory Management Unit (SMMU) so the kernel can schedule work on the Adreno GPU without seeing the underlying hardware differences. All of these pieces live in the `compat/` directory of the repository. The monitor’s entry point is built into a loader that the UEFI firmware hands off to after q1n1 establishes the EL2 proxy. Because the monitor does not modify the kernelcache, the same binary that ships on Apple silicon runs unchanged on the Snapdragon platform. ## Adreno GPU stack replaces Apple’s graphics layer Apple’s graphics stack expects an AGX-style GPU and a corresponding Metal driver. Snapintosh replaces that with a completely native stack for the Adreno X2-90. The stack consists of three components: 1. AdrenoMetal.bundle, a Metal driver plug-in that registers as a Metal device, exposing the same interfaces that applications and WindowServer use. 2. AdrenoX2, an IOGPU kernel extension that implements low-level I/O and memory management for the GPU, including the AdrenoDisplay component that drives the internal panel directly. 3. air2ir3, a shader compiler that translates Apple’s AIR intermediate representation (the format used by Metal) into Mesa’s ir3 format, which the Adreno hardware can execute. The repository’s `gpu/` folder contains the kext sources, the Metal plug-in, and the compiler submodule. The stack runs entirely on the laptop’s own GPU; there is no software, CPU, or paravirtual rendering path. An earlier virtual-AGX model appears in the `gpu/agx*` directory but is kept only for reference. ## USB-C NCM link drives boot and logging from a Mac host Booting the laptop requires a Mac host running macOS 27. The host runs `tools/cycle.py` and a q1n1 proxy client, which together establish a USB-C Network Control Model (NCM) link over the same cable that powers the device. This link carries three critical streams: 1. The monitor image and auxiliary kernelcache (AuxKC) are uploaded from the Mac to the laptop each time it boots. 2. All console output from the EL2 monitor and the early kernel stages is sent back over the NCM link, allowing developers to see what happens before the SSD is mounted. 3. Control commands let the host reset the device, trigger a reboot, or adjust power thresholds. The tools refuse to boot if the laptop’s battery is below a safe level, so AC power is strongly recommended. The flow is visualized in the repository’s `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` with a Mermaid diagram: ```mermaid flowchart TD UEFI["A16 UEFI firmware"] --> Q1N1 Q1N1["q1n1: UEFI EL2 proxy
USB-C NCM link to the Mac host"] --> MON MON["Snapintosh EL2 monitor
SPTM/TXM call emulation, 16K-to-4K shadow page tables"] --> XNU XNU["Stock macOS kernel at EL1 + AuxKC
AdrenoX2 + AdrenoDisplay, SnapI2CHID"] --> USER USER["macOS userspace
WindowServer, Core Animation, apps
AdrenoMetal.bundle + air2ir3 compiler runtime"] HOST["Mac host: tools/cycle.py, q1n1 proxy client"] -. USB-C NCM .-> Q1N1 ``` The diagram shows the linear progression from firmware, through the EL2 proxy, into the monitor, then the kernel and finally userspace. Each arrow represents a handoff that preserves the Apple-expected contracts, while the NCM link remains the only communication channel with the host. ## The takeaway Snapintosh demonstrates that a full macOS boot is possible on non-Apple silicon when a hypervisor supplies the exact platform contracts the kernel expects. By emulating SPTM/TXM calls, translating page tables, and providing a native Adreno Metal driver stack, the project bridges the gap between Apple’s software expectations and Qualcomm’s hardware. Any experiment that needs macOS on a Snapdragon X2 must first implement an EL2 monitor that mirrors Apple’s contracts; without that layer, the stock kernel will not run.

sources.title: Snapintosh/Snapintosh: EL2 hypervisor and toolchain that boots macOS on the ASUS A16 (Snapdragon X2 Elite), with an Adreno Metal/IOGPU stack
